In casual talk people more often say big ego or full of himself, which sound more natural in conversation.

distinctions.note: Egotism is a personal trait or habit; egoism is a philosophical theory that self-interest is the basis of action.
Self-confidence is a healthy belief in your abilities; egotism is an inflated, often annoying sense of your own importance.

examples.everyday: Her constant talking about her new car was pure egotism, and nobody at the party could get a word in.
examples.professional: The manager's egotism made it hard for anyone to share credit or admit a mistake during the project review.
examples.analytical: Egotism, unlike healthy self-regard, rests on a need to be seen as superior, which makes it fragile when others challenge one's standing.

nuance.analogy: Egotism is like a loudspeaker that only plays one song, your own, so nobody else can be heard.
nuance.etymology: From ego, from Latin ego meaning 'I', with the suffix -ism.
common_mistakes: Confusing egotism (a trait) with egoism (a philosophy).
Using egotism as a neutral word for confidence; in American English it nearly always sounds critical.

senses.definition: A person who talks excessively about themself.
A person who believes in their own importance or superiority.
An egoist (advocate of egoism).
senses.example: The philosopher was labeled an egotist by critics who rejected his ethics of self-interest.

core.definition: A person who talks or thinks about themself excessively and believes they are more important than others.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable with a long EE, and keep the second syllable as a weak schwa. Avoid saying ee-GO-tist, which borrows the stress pattern of ego.

nuance.connotation: Negative. Calling someone an egotist criticizes their vanity and self-focus, so it is blunt and works best when the person is not present or with close friends.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use egotist casually for someone who brags or always steers conversations back to themselves, as in 'He's such an egotist.' It is stronger than 'self-centered' and can sound harsh said to someone's face. A softer option is 'He really likes talking about himself.'

distinctions.note: In philosophy, an egoist holds that self-interest is the basis of all action; an egotist is simply vain and self-focused in ordinary behavior.
Narcissist is a clinical-sounding term for a deep, persistent need for admiration; egotist is a looser everyday word for vanity and bragging.

examples.everyday: Jake spent the whole dinner talking about his promotion, and honestly, he's kind of an egotist.
examples.professional: Don't be an egotist in the sprint review; give the analysts credit for the model they built.
examples.analytical: Pascal's account of self-love suggests that the egotist cannot see past his own reflection, even when the truth is in plain view.

nuance.analogy: Like a mirror that only ever shows one face.
nuance.etymology: From Latin ego, 'I', plus the suffix -ist.
common_mistakes: Treating egotist as a neutral description; it is almost always a criticism.
Stressing the second syllable, as in ee-GO-tist.
Confusing egotist with the philosophical term egoist, which has a different meaning.

egotist.etymology: *ego* + -t- inserted to avoid hiatus, or after the analogy of dramatist, epigrammatist, etc.

core.definition: A Hebrew priest, son of Aaron, who succeeded his father as high priest and helped lead Israel after the exodus.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the third syllable, 'ay'. The final er is rhotic and reduced, so say 'zer', not 'zar'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use Eleazar as a personal name in religious settings and in Bible reading. Parents sometimes choose it, and it is pronounced the same way when used as a first name.

distinctions.note: Lazarus is a New Testament name, from the Greek form of the Hebrew name Eleazar, but the two figures are different people.

examples.everyday: My grandfather's middle name is Eleazar, after a priest in the Old Testament.
examples.professional: In the leadership lesson, I used Eleazar as an example of a successor appointed in an orderly way.
examples.analytical: Eleazar's succession of Aaron in Numbers shows how priestly authority passed through a family line.

nuance.analogy: Eleazar is like an heir who takes up a family business after the founder steps down, carrying on the same office.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew El'azar, 'God has helped', from el 'God' and azar 'to help'.
common_mistakes: Confusing Eleazar with Lazarus, who is a different person in the New Testament.
Stressing the second syllable as 'el-ee-AH-zar' rather than the third syllable.
nuance.biblical_note: Hebrew El'azar, 'God has helped'. Eleazar is the son of Aaron. Numbers 3:32 names him chief over the leaders of the Levites who kept the sanctuary. Numbers 20:28 records that Moses put Aaron's garments on Eleazar when Aaron died, so Eleazar became high priest. Joshua 24:33 notes that Eleazar also died and was buried in the hill of Phinehas his son.

senses.definition: Relating to or composed of electors.
Of, or relating to elections.

core.definition: Relating to elections or to voters, especially the Electoral College that formally chooses the president in the United States.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on LEK, the second syllable. The final -oral is pronounced as two weak syllables, 'er-ul', not as 'or-al' with a full vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise political and legal term without emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use electoral almost only as an adjective before a noun, such as electoral college, electoral vote, electoral system or electoral map. It appears often in news about presidential elections, redistricting and voting rules. For the event itself, use 'election'.

distinctions.note: Election is the noun for the event or process of voting; electoral is the adjective describing things related to elections.
Electoral relates to elections or electors; elective means optional or chosen, and in politics describes offices filled by voting.
Electorate is a noun meaning the body of voters; electoral is an adjective that describes things connected with voting or electors.

examples.everyday: Did you see the electoral map on the news? Our county looks solid red.
examples.professional: The communications team must draft a clear explainer on the electoral process before the primary.
examples.analytical: Electoral reform proposals often assume that voters' preferences can be aggregated without distortion, an assumption social choice theory complicates.

nuance.analogy: Like a referee's tally sheet: it turns many individual choices into a single official result.
nuance.etymology: From elector (from Latin eligere 'to choose') with the adjective suffix -al.
common_mistakes: Using electoral as a noun for the vote itself, as in 'the electoral was close'; say 'the election was close'.
Stressing the last syllable, as in 'ee-lek-TOR-al'; the main stress belongs on the second syllable.

senses.definition: The terminal through which electric current passes between metallic and nonmetallic parts of an electric circuit.
senses.example: The electrode carried the current from the battery into the solution.

senses.definition: A collector or emitter of electric charge in a semiconducting device.
senses.example: Engineers doped the electrode region of the transistor to control electron flow.

core.definition: A conductor through which electric current enters or leaves a battery, circuit, device, or other substance.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on LEK, and the first syllable is a short, weak 'ih', not 'ee'. Pronounce the r clearly before the vowel and do not add an extra syllable at the end.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mainly in science, medicine, engineering, and electronics, such as when a nurse attaches electrodes for an ECG. In everyday speech people say 'pads', 'stickers', or 'the wires' for medical or electrical contacts. The word is never rude, but it sounds specialized outside technical settings.

distinctions.note: A terminal is any connection point on a device, while an electrode is specifically a conductor that carries current into or out of a substance, gas, or semiconductor.
An anode is one kind of electrode, the one where oxidation takes place, while a cathode is the other kind, where reduction takes place.
An electron is a subatomic particle that carries negative charge, whereas an electrode is a physical conductor that the charge passes through.

examples.everyday: The nurse put small electrodes on my chest to check my heartbeat.
examples.professional: Before the test, we need to clean the electrodes and check the contact resistance, or the signal will be noisy.
examples.analytical: In an electrochemical cell, the electrode is not merely a conductor but the site where electron transfer defines the reaction.

nuance.analogy: Like a doorway where people enter and leave a building, an electrode is the point where current flows into or out of a substance.
nuance.etymology: Coined by Michael Faraday in 1834 from Greek elektron and hodos, meaning 'way' or 'path'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as 'EE-lek-trode' with a long first vowel; the correct stress is on LEK and the first syllable is weak.
Confusing electrode with electron, the charged particle that moves through the electrode.
Using electrode for any wire; in technical use it means a conductor that passes current into a substance or device.

electrode.etymology: first used in his Diary from the Ancient Greek words *ἤλεκτρον* (“amber”) (from which the word *electricity* is derived) and *ὁδός* (“way”).

senses.definition: Of or having to do with elves; elven.
senses.example: The fantasy novel described elvish villages hidden deep within the misty forest.

core.definition: Of, relating to, or like elves, the magical beings of folklore and fantasy; also the name of Tolkien's invented language.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on EL, and the ending is 'ish' as in 'fish', not 'ee-shuh'. The v is voiced, like the v in 'value'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; can be playful in casual speech.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use elvish in everyday speech, often playfully, to describe a look, a style or a voice, as in an elvish grin. It is also used for the invented language of Tolkien's elves, where it is capitalized as Elvish. Elven is more common in formal fantasy writing, and elfin suggests delicacy.

distinctions.note: Elven is the more formal, literary and fantasy-typical form; elvish is more common in casual talk and in the name Elvish for the language.
Elfin means small, slight or mischievous, often about a child or a face; elvish describes things related to elves in general.

examples.everyday: She has an elvish grin that makes everyone at the party want to know her secret.
examples.professional: The illustrator gave the character elvish features, but the marketing team wants a friendlier version for kids.
examples.analytical: Tolkien's Elvish is not merely decorative; its invented grammar shapes how the characters think about memory and time.

nuance.analogy: Like a sprite in a story: small, quick and slightly beyond normal reach.
nuance.etymology: From elf, from Old English ælf, with the adjectival suffix -ish.
common_mistakes: Spelling it elfish, which is a related but different word meaning mischievous.
Capitalizing elvish for every use; only the name of the language is capitalized.

senses.definition: In the reproductive cycle, the stage after the fertilization of the egg that precedes the development into a fetus.
An organism in the earlier stages of development before it emerges from the egg, or before metamorphosis.
In a viviparous animal, the young animal's earliest stages in the mother's body.
In a human, usually the cell growth of the child within the mother's body, through the end of the seventh week of pregnancy.
senses.example: The doctor explained that the embryo was about the size of a blueberry at eight weeks.

senses.definition: The beginning; the first stage of anything.
senses.example: The idea was only an embryo at that stage, but it grew into our company.

senses.definition: A rudimentary plant contained in the seed.
senses.example: Inside each bean seed lies a tiny embryo that will become the new plant.

core.definition: The earliest stage of an organism's development, after the egg is fertilized and before it becomes recognizable as a fetus or a young animal.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, EM-bree-oh, not em-BREE-oh. The middle vowel is a long 'ee', not 'eye', and the final 'o' is a clear 'oh'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in biology, but charged in American debates about abortion and embryo research, where word choice often signals a moral position.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use embryo mainly in medicine, biology and bioethics. In everyday talk, many people say baby or pregnancy, but a doctor may say the embryo has implanted or is developing. In human development, the term usually covers about the first eight weeks, after which doctors say fetus.

distinctions.note: An embryo is the earlier stage; in humans the term fetus is used from about eight weeks after fertilization until birth.
A zygote is the single fertilized cell; an embryo is the multicellular organism that develops from it.

examples.everyday: My sister and her husband are waiting to hear whether the embryo they froze last year is still viable.
examples.professional: The fertility clinic's report confirmed that the embryo had reached the blastocyst stage and was ready for transfer.
examples.analytical: The moral status of the human embryo is contested, because its potential to become a person does not settle whether it already is one.

nuance.analogy: An embryo is like the first sketch of a building: the basic plan is already there, but the walls and rooms have not yet been built.
nuance.etymology: From Greek embryon, 'that which grows within', from en- 'in' and bryein 'to swell, grow'.
common_mistakes: Saying embryo for any unborn baby at any stage; after about eight weeks in humans, Americans say fetus.
Stressing the second syllable (em-BREE-oh) instead of the first.
nuance.biblical_note: The Bible does not use the word embryo. Psalm 139:16 in the RSV speaks of the psalmist's unformed substance, the Hebrew golem, seen by God before the days were fixed. Psalm 139:13 describes God knitting the psalmist together in the mother's womb. Luke 1:41 and 1:44 describe the unborn John the Baptist leaping in Elizabeth's womb, using the Greek brephos for the unborn child.

embryo.etymology: Borrowed from Medieval Latin *embryō*, from Ancient Greek *ἔμβρυον* (“fetus”), from *ἐν* (“in-”) + *βρύω* (“to grow, swell”).

senses.definition: To invigorate; to make energetic.
To supply with energy, especially electricity; to turn on power to (something).
senses.example: Whenever we energize that circuit we blow a fuse.

core.definition: To give someone or something new energy, or to make them feel more active and lively.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable. The final syllable is a single 'ize' sound that rhymes with 'eyes,' not a separate 'eyes' sound.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests a boost of enthusiasm or vitality, though in technical contexts it can be neutral.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use energize for people, teams, and crowds, as in 'The coffee energized me.' In technical or household contexts, 'turn on' or 'power up' is more common for electronics. In a meeting, saying 'Let's energize the team' sounds natural but a little motivational.

distinctions.note: Motivate focuses on giving someone a reason to act; energize focuses on giving them more vitality or enthusiasm.
Invigorate is more formal and often describes refreshing the body or mind; energize is more common in everyday speech.
Power refers to supplying electricity or force to a device; energize can be used this way too, but in ordinary speech it is more often about people.

examples.everyday: A quick walk after lunch always energizes me before the afternoon.
examples.professional: The new product launch energized the whole sales team and gave us a clear goal for next quarter.
examples.analytical: The sacramental liturgy, in this account, energizes the community by reconnecting it to the source of its life.

nuance.analogy: Energizing someone is like plugging a phone into a charger: the battery goes from low to full.
nuance.etymology: From energy, plus the verb-forming suffix -ize, from Greek -izein.
common_mistakes: Using 'energize' with the wrong stress pattern, saying 'en-er-JIZE' instead of 'EN-er-jyze.'
Confusing energize with energetic; say 'The speech energized the crowd' rather than 'The speech was energetic the crowd.'

senses.definition: In an equal manner; in equal shares or proportion; with equal and impartial justice; evenly.
senses.example: All citizens are equally taxed.

senses.definition: In equal degree or extent; just as.
senses.example: The gas stations are equally far from the highway.

senses.definition: Used to link two or more coordinate elements.
senses.example: John suffered setbacks at his job. Equally, Frank's business slowed.

core.definition: In the same amount or degree for each person or thing; to the same extent.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final -ly is a light 'lee'. The middle syllable is a reduced schwa, so it sounds like 'kwuh'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes fairness or proportion without emotional weight.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use equally in everyday speech to say that things are shared or treated the same way, as in 'equally important'. It is also common in writing and business. In casual talk, 'just as' or 'the same' sounds more natural in some cases. Avoid 'equally as' in formal writing, though it is widespread in conversation.

distinctions.note: Equally shows that two things share the same degree of something, while likewise is used to say 'the same to you' or that someone else does the same thing.
Evenly describes how something is spread or distributed, while equally describes the degree or amount for each person or thing.

examples.everyday: We all pitched in equally, so nobody was stuck with the dishes.
examples.professional: The three proposals are equally viable, so let's decide on cost and timeline.
examples.analytical: Both premises are equally necessary for the argument, and removing either one would make the conclusion fail.

nuance.analogy: Like a pizza cut into exact slices, where every guest gets the same amount.
nuance.etymology: From equal plus the adverbial suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Saying 'equally as good' in formal writing; 'equally good' or 'just as good' is preferred.
Using 'equally' when you mean 'evenly'; equally refers to degree, while evenly refers to distribution.

senses.definition: A daring or adventurous act; an undertaking which goes against convention.
senses.example: Their teenage escapade ended with a midnight swim in the neighbor's forbidden pool.

core.definition: A daring, playful, or slightly reckless adventure, often one that breaks the usual rules or routine.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, ES, and the final syllable rhymes with 'made'. Don't stress the last syllable as in French; the second syllable is a light, unstressed 'kuh'.

nuance.connotation: Usually positive or lighthearted, suggesting fun and a little mischief. It can sound mildly disapproving when it refers to something irresponsible.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'escapade' for a fun, adventurous, or slightly naughty outing, like a teenager sneaking out or friends taking an unplanned road trip. You can say 'That was quite an escapade!' after hearing a story, and a natural reply is 'You're telling me!' or 'Tell me everything.' It is a little old-fashioned in casual speech, so it often sounds warm or humorous.

distinctions.note: An adventure can be serious, long, or heroic, while an escapade is usually shorter, lighter, and a bit mischievous.
An exploit is an impressive, often heroic deed, while an escapade is more playful or reckless.

examples.everyday: Remember that midnight escapade at the lake when we almost got caught?
examples.professional: Our offsite turned into an unplanned escapade when the shuttle broke down, but the team bonded.
examples.analytical: The novel treats the protagonist's escapades as a rebellion against the rigid social order of the period.

nuance.analogy: An escapade is like a detour off the highway of ordinary life, a short side road that is more fun than dangerous.
nuance.etymology: From French 'escapade', from Italian 'scappata', from 'scappare', to escape.
common_mistakes: Stressing the last syllable as in French (es-ca-PADE).
Using 'escapade' for a long, serious journey; it suggests something brief and playful.

escapade.etymology: Borrowed from French *escapade* (“the act of escaping; a trick”), itself borrowed from *escapada*, from *escapar* (“to escape”), from Vulgar Latin **excappō*.

senses.definition: In a eucharistic manner.

core.definition: In a manner relating to the Eucharist, the Christian sacrament of thanksgiving in which bread and wine are received in remembrance of Christ.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on RIS, the third syllable. Learners often stress the first syllable or misplace the -ic ending, which in this word is pronounced -ik-lee.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to reverent. It describes worship or theology and is used with respect in religious settings.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mainly in theological writing, sermons and liturgical discussions. In everyday church talk, people more often say Communion or the Lord's Supper, depending on their tradition. Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican writers use Eucharist, while many Baptists and other Protestants prefer Lord's Supper.

distinctions.note: Sacramentally refers to any sacrament, such as baptism or marriage, while eucharistically refers specifically to the Eucharist or Lord's Supper.
Liturgically describes the form of worship in general, while eucharistically emphasizes the meal of thanksgiving at its center.

examples.everyday: Our parish talks about living eucharistically, which means showing thanks and generosity to our neighbors every day.
examples.professional: The curriculum frames each unit eucharistically, so every lesson connects back to the table of the Lord.
examples.analytical: Augustine reads the church eucharistically, so that the community becomes the body it receives in the sacrament.

nuance.analogy: Living eucharistically is like a family meal where gratitude shapes every relationship at the table.
nuance.etymology: From Greek eucharistia, thanksgiving, from eu, well, and charis, grace or gratitude.
common_mistakes: Confusing eucharistically with sacramentally, which covers all sacraments.
Stressing the first syllable as in YOO-kuh-ris-tik-lee.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek word eucharistia means thanksgiving. It appears in the Gospel accounts of the Last Supper, such as Luke 22:19, where Jesus gives thanks over the bread before sharing it with his disciples. Paul in 1 Corinthians 11:23-26 describes the Lord's Supper as a remembrance of Christ's death until he comes, linking the act of thanksgiving to proclamation.

traditions.view: The Eucharist is the central mystery of the Divine Liturgy, in which the bread and wine become the body and blood of Christ. It is received by all baptized members, including infants, and is understood as participation in the life of the whole church.

The Eucharist is the sacrament in which, through transubstantiation, the bread and wine become the body and blood of Christ. It is offered as sacrifice in the Mass and presided over by an ordained priest.

Most Protestants call it the Lord's Supper and differ on the presence of Christ: Lutherans teach Christ's real presence in, with and under the bread and wine; Reformed churches teach a spiritual presence for believers; and many Baptists and other churches see it as a memorial.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to eudaemonism.

core.definition: Relating to eudaemonism, the view that happiness comes from virtue and living well, rather than from pleasure alone.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on NIS, the fourth syllable. Learners often stress the -DEE- from the noun, but the adjective moves the stress to -NIS-.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise philosophical term with no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this adjective when describing a theory or argument in ethics or classical philosophy. It is rarely heard outside academic settings. For a casual description, people would say focused on living well or virtue-based.

distinctions.note: Hedonistic describes a focus on pleasure as the highest good, while eudaemonistic describes a focus on flourishing through virtue.
Eudaemonic is a broader adjective that can describe well-being in psychology, while eudaemonistic specifically refers to the ethical theory.

collocations: eudaemonistic account of the good life

examples.professional: Our ethics review uses a eudaemonistic framework, which asks whether a product helps users grow rather than just whether they feel satisfied.
examples.analytical: Aquinas' ethics is eudaemonistic in structure, because it locates human happiness in the perfection of human nature through virtue and grace.

nuance.analogy: A eudaemonistic view is like judging a meal by its nourishment rather than its taste.
nuance.etymology: Formed in English from eudaemonism with the adjective suffix -istic.
common_mistakes: Using eudaemonistic as a synonym for hedonistic, which means the opposite.
Stressing the first syllable or the -DEE- as in YOO-dee-muh-nis-tik.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to euphuism.
senses.example: His euphuistic prose, full of balanced antitheses, made the simple letter sound ornate.

core.definition: Overly ornate and artificial in style, full of balanced antitheses, alliteration and elaborate similes.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on the IS syllable, with a light secondary stress on the first syllable. Keep the final -ic as a short 'ik' sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative in most contexts. It criticizes writing or speech that is showy and mannered rather than clear.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word in literary criticism, academic writing and sometimes in sharp professional feedback about overwritten documents. In casual conversation it sounds stiff or pretentious. A plainer alternative such as 'flowery' or 'overwrought' is usually more natural in everyday American speech.

distinctions.note: Flowery is common and general, describing any ornate language. Euphuistic is narrower, referring to a specific style of balanced antitheses and alliteration.
Euphemistic means using polite substitute words to soften a harsh idea. Euphuistic means ornate in structure and sound, so the two are often confused but mean different things.

examples.everyday: Stop talking so euphuistic and just tell me when dinner will be ready.
examples.professional: The grant proposal reads as euphuistic, so reviewers cannot find the plain statement of our methods.
examples.analytical: Lyly's euphuistic style depends on antithesis, parallel clauses and classical allusion to produce its characteristic rhythm.

nuance.analogy: Euphuistic writing is like a building where every surface is carved, so the structure is hard to see under the decoration.
nuance.etymology: Derived from euphuism, which comes from Euphues, the title character of John Lyly's 1578 novel.
common_mistakes: Confusing euphuistic with euphemistic, which concerns polite substitute words rather than ornate style.
Stressing the second syllable of yoo-fyoo-IS-tik, which makes the word hard to recognize.

senses.definition: Liable to cause disapproval, objection or debate.

core.definition: Likely to be objected to or criticized; open to disapproval or debate.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on 'SEP,' with a light 'shun' and a strong secondary-like 'AY' in the suffix. The final syllable is a reduced 'bul.'

nuance.connotation: Negative; it signals that something is problematic or inappropriate.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use exceptionable in speech. It appears in formal writing, legal or diplomatic language, and older prose. In everyday talk people say 'objectionable,' 'offensive,' or 'questionable.' The word is often used in negative phrases like 'not exceptionable,' meaning acceptable.

distinctions.note: Objectionable is the everyday equivalent and is much more common in American speech.
Exceptional means outstanding, while exceptionable means open to objection; the words look similar but have opposite connotations.

examples.professional: The draft contained wording the legal team found exceptionable, so we revised it before sending.
examples.analytical: The author's use of the term is exceptionable because it blurs a distinction the argument depends on.

nuance.analogy: Like a sentence with a red flag on it, waiting for someone to object.
nuance.etymology: From exception, from Latin exceptio, plus the suffix -able, 'capable of being.'
common_mistakes: Confusing 'exceptionable' with 'exceptional'; one means objectionable, the other means outstanding.
Using 'exceptionable' in casual speech, where 'objectionable' sounds more natural.

senses.definition: Human and non-human animal solid waste excreted from the bowels; feces.

core.definition: Solid waste that the body eliminates through the bowels; feces, or animal waste when used for animals.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, EKS, which differs from excrete (ik-SKREET), where the stress moves to the second syllable. The middle syllable is a weak 'kruh', and the final -ment is a reduced 'muhnt'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in medical or scientific contexts, but crude or unpleasant in everyday use. Its clinical tone can sound stiff in casual talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely say excrement in conversation. Casually they say 'poop', and parents often say 'poo' with children; doctors say 'stool' or 'feces'; farmers use 'manure' for animal waste. Excrement is most common in writing, biology, or environmental reports about animal waste.

distinctions.note: Feces is the clinical and scientific term for solid human waste; excrement is a broader word that also covers animal waste and other excreted matter.
Manure is animal waste used as fertilizer, a farming term; excrement is a general term and does not imply agricultural use.
Waste is a general word for anything discarded; excrement specifically refers to matter excreted by a body.

examples.everyday: There was bird excrement all over the bench near the park, so I walked around it.
examples.professional: The water-quality report flagged high bacterial levels from animal excrement upstream of the creek intake.
examples.analytical: Some ancient societies burned dried animal excrement as fuel, which shows how closely waste, survival, and resource use were tied together.

nuance.analogy: Like the body's shipping department: it sends out what the body has finished using.
nuance.etymology: From Latin excrementum 'that which is sifted out', from excernere 'to sift out', from ex- 'out' plus cernere 'to separate'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, as in ex-KREH-muhnt, which confuses it with the verb excrete.
Using excrement in casual conversation where poop is the natural word, which sounds clinical or stiff.

senses.definition: The act of extemporizing; the act of doing anything extempore.
senses.example: Her extemporization during the debate impressed the judges, who had expected a prepared speech.

core.definition: The act of improvising or speaking, playing, or performing something on the spot without advance preparation or a written plan.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on ZAY, with a lighter stress on the first syllable. The verb extemporize stresses the first syllable, so the stress shifts in the noun. The ending -ation is pronounced shun.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It can praise a speaker's or musician's skill, but it can also describe improvised work that feels rough.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use extemporization mostly in music, theology, speech training, and academic discussion, where it names the skill or act of improvising. In everyday conversation people say improvising or winging it. The word sounds more formal and learned than improvisation, which is the usual choice in American English.

distinctions.note: Improvisation is the common word for spontaneous creation in music, theater, and life, while extemporization is more formal and often used for speech or prayer.
Preparation is planned work done in advance, so it is the opposite of extemporization.

examples.everyday: The kids' play had a lot of extemporization, so the story changed every time we watched it.
examples.professional: Our product demo relied on some extemporization when the internet connection dropped, and the team handled it well.
examples.analytical: Some theologians argue that extemporization in prayer reveals the speaker's sincere dependence on God rather than mere eloquence.

nuance.analogy: Like a cook who makes a good meal from whatever is left in the refrigerator, without a recipe.
nuance.etymology: From extemporize, from Latin ex tempore 'on the spur of the moment', from ex 'from' plus tempore 'time'.
common_mistakes: Using extemporization as a countable noun for many separate acts; it is usually uncountable.
Stressing the first syllable in the noun as you would in the verb extemporize.

senses.definition: Any of various mechanical devices that extract a component from others.
senses.example: The cafeteria bought a new industrial extractor to pull grease and smoke out of the kitchen air.

senses.definition: A machine for clearing combs of honey.
A device for rendering wax.
A centrifugal drying machine.
senses.example: After the wash cycle, we loaded the wet salad greens into the extractor to spin off the water.

senses.definition: A part of the bolt that removes a cartridge from the chamber.
senses.example: Check that the extractor has gripped the rim, because a loose extractor can jam the next round.

senses.definition: A particular kind of bipartite graph.
senses.example: The lemma constructs a bipartite extractor whose expansion ensures every large left subset reaches many right vertices.

senses.definition: A function which, being applied to output from a weakly random entropy source, together with a short, uniformly random seed, generates a highly random output that appears independent from the source and uniformly distributed.
senses.example: The cryptographer proved that the extractor turns a weak random source and a short seed into nearly uniform bits.

senses.definition: An apparatus that uses a solvent to remove soluble substances from a mixture.
senses.example: The chemist used a Soxhlet extractor to pull caffeine out of the ground coffee with ethanol.

core.definition: A machine or device that removes a component, substance, or product from something else, such as honey from a comb.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, STRAK, and the final -or is a reduced, unstressed American er sound, not oh. Many learners stress the first syllable or add a strong final vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a purely descriptive technical term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Beekeepers use extractor for the drum machine that spins honey out of combs, and it appears in many other fields such as chemistry labs and DNA work. In American homes, the ceiling or wall fan that pulls air out of a kitchen or bathroom is called an exhaust fan or vent fan, not an extractor fan, which is the British term.

distinctions.note: An extractor pulls a particular substance out of a mixture, while a separator divides a mixture into its parts, often by density or spinning.
A juicer is a kitchen appliance for fruit and vegetables, whereas an extractor is a broader term for any device that pulls out a component.

examples.everyday: Our neighbor borrowed the honey extractor from the club, so we're spinning our frames this weekend.
examples.professional: The lab's new solvent extractor cut our sample prep time in half, so we can run more batches each day.
examples.analytical: The author treats the extractor as a metaphor for institutional power, drawing out value while leaving the source depleted.

nuance.analogy: An extractor works like a strainer that pulls out only one ingredient and leaves the rest behind.
nuance.etymology: From Latin extractus, past participle of extrahere, meaning to draw out.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as EK-stract-or instead of ik-STRAK-ter.
Using extractor for the American exhaust fan, which Americans call an exhaust fan or vent fan.

senses.definition: Known only in fables; fictitious.
senses.example: The fabled dragon of the old tale never existed outside the storyteller's imagination.

senses.definition: Made known by fables or reputation; legendary, famed.
senses.example: The fabled jazz club on Beale Street still draws tourists from around the world.

core.definition: Famous and legendary, often described in stories or reputation, sometimes even fictional.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on FAY. The ending is a reduced vowel followed by d, so it is one short syllable at the end, not two.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests admiration and mystery, though it can also suggest that something is more legend than fact.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use fabled in writing, reviews, speeches and storytelling to describe places, people or events that have become legendary, such as a fabled restaurant or a fabled season. It is less common in casual talk, where people would say famous or legendary. Use it when you want a touch of romance or myth.

distinctions.note: Famous is plain and general, while fabled suggests a reputation built over time through stories.
Legendary is more common in everyday speech and can be used for living people, while fabled sounds more literary and often refers to places or things of the past.

examples.everyday: We drove past the fabled taco stand everybody talks about, but it was closed on Mondays.
examples.professional: Our operations team still talks about the fabled outage of 2014 as the reason we built better alerts.
examples.analytical: The fabled Garden of Eden in Genesis functions less as a map than as a theological symbol of human origins.

nuance.analogy: A fabled place is like a town in a bedtime story: everyone knows its name, but few have actually seen it.
nuance.etymology: From fable, from Latin fabula, 'story.'
common_mistakes: Using fabled only to mean false; it usually means famous or legendary, though it can refer to fiction.
Stressing the second syllable or adding an extra syllable at the end.

senses.definition: Something that facilitates.
senses.example: The new software is a useful facilitator for sharing data between our research teams.

senses.definition: A person who helps a group to have an effective dialog without taking any side of the argument, especially in order to reach a consensus.
senses.example: The church hired a facilitator to help the board discuss the budget dispute fairly.

core.definition: A person who guides a group discussion neutrally so it can reach agreement or a decision.

pronunciation.tip: Stress SIL, with a weak 'uh' in the first syllable. The final syllable is 'tur,' a rhotic r sound that Americans pronounce clearly.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it describes a neutral, helpful role in a meeting or workshop.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use facilitator for a person who runs workshops, team meetings or training sessions without taking sides. The word is common in offices, schools and nonprofits. A natural reply when someone asks for help is 'Sure, I can act as facilitator for the meeting.'

distinctions.note: A moderator keeps order in a debate or panel, while a facilitator helps a group reach its own agreement.
A chair has authority over the meeting and makes decisions, while a facilitator usually does not decide the outcome.

examples.everyday: My friend works as a facilitator for a community group, so she helps neighbors settle their disagreements.
examples.professional: We hired an outside facilitator to run the retrospective so everyone could speak freely.
examples.analytical: A good facilitator suspends personal opinion so the group can examine its own assumptions.

nuance.analogy: A facilitator is like a referee who helps players talk through the rules rather than telling them who should win.
nuance.etymology: From facilitate, with the agent suffix -or.
common_mistakes: Putting the main stress on the last syllable instead of SIL.
Using facilitator to mean the person who makes the final decision.

conversation.text: Ana will be our facilitator today, so she'll keep us on time.
A good facilitator makes sure the quiet people get a chance to talk.
We hired an outside facilitator for the strategy offsite.

senses.definition: An expression used to concede a point, but suggesting that the broader argument is incorrect.
senses.example: You can play the exercises pretty well on piano, fair enough, but can you play the movement expressively?

senses.definition: Used to acknowledge a person's point or argument; denotes that, upon consideration, something is correct or reasonable; an expression of acknowledgment or understanding.
senses.example: You think the model overfits? Fair enough, let's add cross-validation before we ship it.

core.definition: Used to accept someone's point as reasonable, even if you still have a small reservation or disagree a little.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on ENOUGH. In fast speech the words link into 'fair-ih-NUF', so do not pause between them or insert an extra vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It signals fair-minded acceptance, though said flatly it can sound dismissive.
nuance.usage_note: Very common in American conversation to accept a point or a decision: 'I'll skip dessert.' 'Fair enough.' Said with a shrug and a warm tone, it closes a discussion politely. Said flatly, it can sound like you stopped listening, so soften your voice; a natural reply is 'Yeah, sounds good.'

distinctions.note: 'That makes sense' shows you understand the reasoning; 'fair enough' accepts the point, sometimes reluctantly.
'Okay' is neutral and can mean nothing more; 'fair enough' implies you considered the other person's reasons.

examples.everyday: You don't want to see that movie? Fair enough, we can watch something else.
examples.professional: Fair enough, let's push the launch to next sprint and revisit the data quality issue then.
examples.analytical: That is fair enough as far as it goes, but the argument still assumes the sample was representative.

nuance.analogy: A referee's shrug: he accepts the call without claiming the rule is perfect.
common_mistakes: Treating 'fair enough' as a question asking for an opinion; it is a response that closes a point.
Saying just 'fair' in casual speech when you mean 'fair enough'; the short form sounds unfinished.

conversation.text: "I can't come; I have to work early." "Fair enough. Next time."
Fair enough. You did warn me it would be cold.
"I'd rather drive myself." "Fair enough, I'll meet you there."

senses.definition: In a fallacious manner, erroneously, illogically.

core.definition: In a way that is based on a false or faulty argument; erroneously or illogically.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, LAY. The 'ci' in the middle is pronounced like 'sh', and the final -ly is quick and unstressed.

nuance.connotation: Negative: it signals that reasoning is flawed, often in a critical or corrective context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mainly in academic writing, debate, law, and philosophy when pointing out faulty reasoning. In conversation people usually say 'that's not logical' or 'that doesn't follow' instead. It can sound stiff in casual talk.

distinctions.note: 'Wrongly' refers to any mistake, while 'fallaciously' specifically means reasoning that appears valid but is not.
'Illogically' is more general and everyday, while 'fallaciously' names a specific kind of faulty argument.

examples.everyday: My uncle reasoned fallaciously that because he never got sick after eating kale, kale must cure colds.
examples.professional: The report fallaciously concluded that the drop in sales caused the new hiring policy, without checking any other factors.
examples.analytical: The critic argues fallaciously that because moral progress has occurred alongside technology, technology must be the cause of moral progress.

nuance.analogy: Like a bridge built on a cracked beam: it looks sturdy, but the conclusion collapses under weight.
nuance.etymology: From Latin fallax, 'deceptive,' from fallere, 'to deceive.'
common_mistakes: Using it to mean 'falsely' about facts rather than about reasoning.
Pronouncing the middle 'ci' as 'see' instead of 'sh'.

senses.definition: An informal fallacy applying to inductive arguments, in which the similarity in one respect of two concepts, objects, or events is taken as sufficient to establish that they are similar in another respect in which they actually are dissimilar.
senses.example: Your argument reposes on false analogies.

core.definition: An argument error in which two things are called alike in one respect, so they are assumed to be alike in another respect where they actually differ.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on NAL, the same as in analogous. Say the first vowel of false as the open aw sound, and make the unstressed syllables short and reduced.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It names a flaw in reasoning, so calling an argument a false analogy is a criticism of the logic, not of the person.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this term in debates, editorials, classrooms and workplace arguments to point out a weak comparison. In casual talk people more often say bad comparison or that's not the same thing. Using false analogy at a dinner table can sound like debate-club language, but it is perfectly normal in serious discussion.

distinctions.note: A false cause assumes that one event caused another just because it came first; a false analogy assumes that two cases match in a relevant way when they do not.
A hasty generalization draws a broad conclusion from too few cases; a false analogy draws a conclusion from one comparison that is not really similar.

examples.everyday: That's a false analogy, Dan. A country isn't a household, so you can't balance its budget the same way.
examples.professional: Saying our new model works like the old one is a false analogy, because the data pipeline and the features are completely different.
examples.analytical: The argument from the organism to the state is a false analogy, since biological and political bodies differ in exactly the respects the conclusion needs.

nuance.analogy: Like judging a fish by how well it climbs trees: the comparison sounds clever, but the skill it measures has nothing to do with the fish's real abilities.
nuance.etymology: From Greek analogia, proportion, from ana- according to and logos ratio or reason.
common_mistakes: Using false analogy to mean any wrong comparison; the term means a comparison whose similarity does not support the conclusion.
Stressing the wrong syllable in analogy, saying uh-NAL-uh-jee versus AN-uh-lo-jee.

senses.definition: To alter so as to make false; especially when done with intent to deceive.
senses.example: to falsify a record or document

senses.definition: To misrepresent.
senses.example: The accountant was fired after she falsified the quarterly reports to hide losses.

senses.definition: To counterfeit; to forge.
senses.example: to falsify money

senses.definition: To show (an item of charge inserted in an account) to be wrong.
senses.example: The auditor falsified the duplicate charge once she confirmed the hotel had billed it twice.

core.definition: To change information or records on purpose so that they are false, usually in order to deceive people.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, and the second syllable is a weak schwa, so the middle sounds like suh. The final syllable rhymes with my, with a clear diphthong.

nuance.connotation: Negative
nuance.usage_note: Americans use falsify for serious deception involving documents, data, records, or evidence, as in news reports, audits, or court cases. In casual talk people usually say fake or make up. Accusing someone of falsifying records is a strong charge that has legal and professional consequences.

distinctions.note: Fake is informal and can refer to objects or appearances; falsify refers to altering information or records with intent to deceive.
Misreport can be an honest mistake, while falsify implies deliberate deception.

examples.everyday: My uncle got in trouble at work because somebody said he falsified his expense reports to get extra money.
examples.professional: Any analyst who falsifies data for a dashboard will be terminated and may be reported to compliance.
examples.analytical: To falsify a result is not merely to be wrong, but to alter the evidence so that the record no longer reflects what was observed.

nuance.analogy: Falsifying a record is like changing the numbers on a clock so that everyone shows up at the wrong time, and the whole schedule runs on lies.
nuance.etymology: From Latin falsificare, to make false, from falsus, false, and facere, to make.
common_mistakes: Using falsify for an honest error; it always implies intent.
Stressing the second syllable, which sounds unnatural.

falsify.etymology: From French *falsifier*, from Late Latin *falsificō* (“make false, corrupt, counterfeit, falsify”), from Latin *falsificus*, from *falsus* (“false”), corresponding to *false* + *ify*.

senses.definition: Distant; remote in space.
senses.example: He went to a far land.

senses.definition: Remote in time.
senses.example: the far far future

senses.definition: Long. (Can we add an example for this sense?)
senses.example: The rope ran far across the creek, long enough to reach the old oak tree.

senses.definition: More remote of two.
senses.example: See those two mountains? The ogre lives on the far one.

senses.definition: Extreme, as measured from some central or neutral position.
senses.example: They are on the far right on this issue.

senses.definition: Extreme, as a difference in nature or quality.
senses.example: There is a far difference between a good plan and a great one.

senses.definition: Outside the currently selected segment in a segmented memory architecture.
senses.example: far heap; far memory; far pointer

senses.definition: To, from or over a great distance in space, time or other extent.
senses.example: You have all come far and you will go further.

senses.definition: Very much; by a great amount.
senses.example: He was far richer than we'd thought.

senses.definition: Emmer (a type of wheat), especially in the context of Roman use of it.
senses.example: The museum display described far, an ancient wheat, as the staple grain of Roman soldiers.

senses.definition: (rare) To send far away.
senses.example: The sudden gust seemed to far the kite beyond the hills.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: To or at a great distance in space or time; used in questions like how far and in negatives like not far.

pronunciation.tip: Pronounce the r clearly in American English, because the vowel is an r-colored ar sound. Do not drop the r as in some British accents, and do not confuse far with fur.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a basic, everyday word used in questions and statements about distance.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use far most often in questions and negatives, such as How far is it? or It's not far. In affirmative statements, they often prefer a long way, a long distance, or far away, which sound more natural in casual speech. Far is also common in comparisons, such as far better and far too expensive.

distinctions.note: Distant is more formal and often describes physical or emotional remoteness, while far is the everyday neutral word for distance.
Farther is for physical distance, while further refers to extent, time, or an additional amount, as in further questions.

examples.everyday: How far is the airport from your house?
examples.professional: We are not far from the deadline, so let's keep the scope tight.
examples.analytical: The argument goes far beyond the evidence, which is what makes it persuasive yet weak.

nuance.analogy: A ruler laid out between two points: far is how long the measure is.
nuance.etymology: From Old English feorr, meaning distant or remote.
common_mistakes: Saying fur or fair for far, which changes the vowel.
Using far in affirmative sentences where a long way or far away sounds more natural in casual speech, as in I walked a long way.

far.etymology: Middle English *ferre*, *fer*, Old English *feor*, *feorr*, from Proto-Germanic **ferrai*.

senses.definition: To or at a great distance.
senses.example: She lived far away, in a distant land.

core.definition: At or to a great distance from the place where you are or are speaking.

pronunciation.tip: Both words get some stress, but AWAY is the main stress, so the word 'away' is louder and longer than 'far'. Keep the r in 'far' strongly pronounced, and reduce the 'a' in 'away' to a quick uh sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes distance without judgment, and can sound warm or wistful depending on context, such as someone missing a faraway family member.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'far away' constantly for both physical and emotional distance, such as 'My parents live far away.' It can also modify a noun in the form 'faraway,' as in 'a faraway land,' but in the adverb form, keep the two words separate. For a more casual or vague sense, Americans often say 'way out there' or 'way out in the boonies.'

distinctions.note: Almost identical in meaning, but 'far off' is slightly more common when describing something seen in the distance, while 'far away' is more common for places where people live or go.
'Distant' is an adjective and sounds more formal or literary; Americans would more naturally say 'far away' in conversation.

examples.everyday: My sister lives far away, in Oregon, so we only see each other twice a year.
examples.professional: Our data engineers are far away in another time zone, so we hand off work through the ticket queue overnight.
examples.analytical: The ideal of justice can seem far away when we look at how the suffering of the poor is ignored in public debate.

nuance.analogy: Think of a lighthouse on a distant coast: you can see it, but it is far away from where you stand.
nuance.etymology: 'Far' comes from Old English feorr, and 'away' comes from Old English aweg, meaning 'on the way' or 'off.'
common_mistakes: Writing 'faraway' as an adverb in a sentence like 'He moved faraway'; the one-word form is an adjective, so use 'far away' after a verb.
Saying 'far from' when you mean 'far away,' as in 'far from here' is fine but 'far away here' is not.

senses.definition: Resembling a farce; ludicrous; absurd.
senses.example: The courtroom testimony became farcical when the witness kept mixing up the defendant's name.

core.definition: Absurd and ridiculous, so badly handled or unreasonable that it looks like a poorly written comedy.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, FAR. The middle vowel is a reduced 'uh', so the word has three syllables, not four.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It suggests that something is absurd, unfair, or poorly managed.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use farcical to describe political, legal, or bureaucratic failures in news and formal writing. It is stronger and more formal than 'ridiculous' and sounds like careful criticism. In casual speech people often say 'ridiculous' or 'a joke' instead.

distinctions.note: Ridiculous is broader and more casual. Farcical suggests a situation so badly organized that it resembles a bad comedy.
Absurd suggests something logically contradictory or senseless. Farcical emphasizes the chaotic, comic failure of a situation.
Comical means funny, sometimes in a lighthearted way. Farcical is critical and implies the situation should not have happened.

examples.everyday: The parking situation at this mall is farcical, and I spent twenty minutes just looking for a spot.
examples.professional: The timeline we were given is farcical, since the testing alone takes three weeks.
examples.analytical: The claim that the proof is complete without the lemma is farcical, because that gap is the whole problem.

nuance.analogy: Like a plot in which every character makes the wrong decision and the audience can see the disaster coming.
nuance.etymology: From farce, with the suffix -ical meaning having the nature of.
common_mistakes: Using farcical as a noun; the noun is farce.
Pronouncing it with a long 'a' as in 'far-SICK-al'.

senses.definition: The quality of being fateful.

core.definition: The quality of being fateful, that is, of having major and possibly irreversible consequences.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on FAYT. The -ful and -ness endings are both reduced, so they sound like fuhl and nuhs, not full vowels.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to somber. It describes a sense of weight or irreversibility in a situation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use fatefulness in everyday speech. It appears mainly in essays, literature, and formal analysis. In normal conversation, people say 'the significance of the moment' or 'how important it was.'

distinctions.note: Significance is general importance; fatefulness suggests consequences that cannot be undone.
Gravity emphasizes seriousness; fatefulness emphasizes that the outcome will shape what comes after.

examples.professional: The fatefulness of the vote is clear, since one dissenting partner could block the merger.
examples.analytical: Heidegger's notion of destiny (Schicksal) ties individual existence to the fatefulness of a shared historical inheritance.

nuance.analogy: Fatefulness is like the weight of a door swinging shut behind you: once it closes, you cannot go back through it.
nuance.etymology: From fateful, with the noun suffix -ness, from fate (from Latin fatum).
common_mistakes: Using fatefulness to describe a person; say 'a fateful person' only rarely, or better, use another adjective.
Using fatefulness in casual speech where significance or importance would be more natural.

senses.definition: Synonym of antipyretic (“a fever-reducing medication”).

core.definition: A medicine that reduces fever; a fever-reducing drug, also called an antipyretic.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the middle syllable is a reduced 'rih'. The final sound is a soft 'j' as in 'huge', not a separate 'ghe' syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise clinical word with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mainly in medical, pharmacy, and scientific writing. In everyday conversation people say fever reducer, or name the product, such as Tylenol or Advil. Using febrifuge at home sounds technical rather than rude.

distinctions.note: The two words are synonyms; antipyretic is the more common term in medical and pharmacy contexts.
An analgesic relieves pain, while a febrifuge specifically lowers body temperature; many drugs do both.

examples.everyday: My doctor said to take something over the counter to bring my fever down, a febrifuge like Tylenol.
examples.professional: Please confirm whether the febrifuge we stock is approved for children under twelve before we fill the order.
examples.analytical: Cinchona bark served as a febrifuge long before anyone understood the chemistry behind its effect.

nuance.analogy: A febrifuge is like a thermostat turned down: it lowers the heat without fixing the cause of the fire.
nuance.etymology: From Latin febris (fever) and fugare (to drive away).
common_mistakes: Confusing febrifuge (a medicine) with febrile (having a fever).
Stressing the final syllable instead of the first.

senses.definition: To grope; to explore an area with one's hands, usually in search of something.
senses.example: I felt around in my pockets for my keyring in vain.

senses.definition: To gather information sneakily; to seek out information without revealing that one is actively searching for it.
senses.example: Before revealing his plans, the detective began to feel around for gossip among the hotel staff.

core.definition: To search for something by moving your hands over a surface, especially in the dark; informally, to try to learn information without asking directly.

pronunciation.tip: The particle 'around' gets the main stress in this phrasal verb, while 'feel' is secondary. The first vowel of 'around' is reduced, so it is close to 'uh-ROWND'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative, depending on context. The physical sense is neutral; the informal sense of seeking information covertly can suggest a bit of sneakiness.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say feel around for keys in a dark room or feel around for a light switch. In casual talk, people also use it to mean trying to find out what someone thinks without asking directly. It is informal, so it fits conversation with friends and colleagues but not formal writing.

distinctions.note: Grope suggests clumsy, blind searching and can imply sexual touching; feel around describes more neutral, careful exploration.
Feel out means to test someone's opinion or reaction, and is close to this sense, but it is more direct and deliberate than feel around.

collocations: feel around for the light switch

examples.everyday: I had to feel around for my keys in the dark because the porch light was out.
examples.professional: Before the meeting, I felt around to see whether the director would support the budget change.
examples.analytical: Rather than state the thesis openly, the author feels around the question, letting readers infer the position from the examples.

nuance.analogy: It is like a hand moving through a dark closet, touching shelves and boxes until it finds what it wants.
nuance.etymology: Feel from Old English fēlan; around from Middle English aboute with the same sense of circling.
common_mistakes: Dropping 'around' and saying 'feel for keys' when you mean searching physically; 'feel for' has a different meaning.
Putting the stress on 'feel' in casual speech, which can make the phrase sound like a different verb.

senses.definition: An ornament such as a garland or chain which hangs loosely from two tacked spots.
senses.example: The wedding hall was draped with a festoon of white roses hanging between the chandeliers.

senses.definition: A bas-relief, painting, or structural motif resembling such an ornament.
senses.example: The cathedral's stone frieze carried a carved festoon of fruit and ribbons above each arch.

senses.definition: A raised cable with light globes attached.
senses.example: An electrician hung a festoon of bulbs across the patio for the summer party.

senses.definition: Any of a series of wrinkles on the backs of some ticks.
senses.example: Under the microscope, the tick's back showed a row of festoons near its rear edge.

senses.definition: A specific style of electric light bulb consisting of a cylindrical enclosure with two points of contact on either end providing power to the filament or diode.
senses.example: The old kitchen ceiling still used a festoon bulb that gave off a warm amber glow.

senses.definition: Two sets of rollers used to create a buffer of material on web handling equipment.
senses.example: The press operator adjusted the festoon between the rollers to keep the paper web from snapping.

senses.definition: Any of various papilionid butterflies of the genus Zerynthia.
senses.example: Entomologists photographed a festoon butterfly drifting over the limestone slopes near Dubrovnik.

senses.definition: A cloud on Jupiter that hangs out of its home belt or zone into an adjacent area forming a curved finger-like image or a complete loop back to its home belt or zone.
senses.example: Amateur astronomers noticed a bright festoon curling out of Jupiter's South Equatorial Belt last month.

senses.definition: Texturing applied to a denture to simulate human tissue.
senses.example: The dental technician added a stippled festoon to the denture base so it looked like gum tissue.

senses.definition: To decorate as if with ornaments, such as garlands or chains, which hang loosely from two tacked spots.
senses.example: The volunteers festooned the community center with paper lanterns and green garlands for the festival.

senses.definition: To make festoons.
To decorate or bedeck abundantly.
senses.example: He was bewildered by how the car was festooned with polka dots.

senses.definition: To apply texturing to (a denture) to simulate human tissue.
senses.example: The technician festooned the denture base with fine stippling to mimic the gum line.

core.definition: To decorate something by hanging garlands, ribbons, lights or chains in loops between points. Usually used in the passive: festooned with.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, which has a long "oo" as in "moon." The first syllable is short, as in "fess." Don't stress the first syllable, which is a common mistake.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It suggests cheerful, elaborate decoration.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use festoon mostly in writing or descriptive speech about decorations with lights, streamers or flowers. In everyday talk, people more often say "decorate" or "hang things up," so festoon can sound a bit fancy. It is most common in the passive form, as in "the hall was festooned with balloons."

distinctions.note: Decorate is the general everyday word for making something look nicer. Festoon specifically means hanging decorations in loops or swags.
Garland is a noun for a wreath or chain of flowers or leaves. Festoon is the verb for decorating with such things.

examples.everyday: The porch was festooned with paper lanterns for the backyard party.
examples.professional: Our booth at the trade show was festooned with banners, LED strips and logo stickers.
examples.analytical: Baroque churches were often festooned with carved fruit and cherubs, turning architecture into a theater of abundance.

nuance.analogy: Like a clothesline strung with ribbons that sag in loops, a festooned room looks decorated in swooping curves.
nuance.etymology: From Italian festone, a garland, from festa, festival.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as "FES-toon"
Forgetting the preposition: say "festooned with lights," not "festooned lights" in the passive
Using it for any decoration, when it specifically means hanging loops of decoration

senses.definition: A result of research or an investigation.
A formal conclusion by a judge, jury or regulatory agency on issues of fact.
senses.example: The jury's finding that the company had misled investors surprised almost everyone in court.

senses.definition: That which is found, a find, a discovery.
senses.example: My best finding this year was a first edition of Melville in a thrift store.

senses.definition: The act of discovering something by chance, an instance of finding something by chance.
senses.example: Her finding of the lost ring under the couch cushions was pure luck.

senses.definition: Tools or materials used in shoe making or repair.
senses.example: The repair shop stocked heels, glue, and every finding a cobbler might need.

senses.definition: A self-contained component of assembled jewelry.
senses.example: She bought silver findings, clasps and jump rings, to finish her earrings.

core.definition: A result or conclusion reached through research, an investigation, or an official review.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, and the second syllable is a short, unstressed 'ih' sound, not a long 'ee.' Keep the 'ng' as one sound at the end, without adding a 'g' after it.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'finding' in research, science, business reports, and legal or regulatory settings to mean a specific result or conclusion. In casual talk people say 'result' or 'what we learned' instead. In a formal setting, saying 'the main finding' signals that a carefully supported conclusion is being presented.

distinctions.note: A 'result' can be any outcome, while a 'finding' is a conclusion reached through investigation or analysis.
A 'conclusion' is the final judgment drawn from reasoning, while a 'finding' is usually a specific observed or established result.

examples.everyday: My doctor said the blood test showed a surprising finding, so she wants me to come back next week.
examples.professional: Our analysis confirmed the main finding: customer churn rises sharply after the third month of use.
examples.analytical: The paper's central finding is that trust, rather than price, best explains long-term loyalty across these markets.

nuance.analogy: A finding is like a fossil uncovered after careful digging: the work reveals something that was there all along, waiting to be recognized.
nuance.etymology: From find (Old English findan) plus the suffix -ing, used to form nouns from verbs.
common_mistakes: Using 'finding' as a synonym for 'discovery' in casual speech, when 'discovery' is more common for something new and exciting.
Using the singular 'a finding' when the plural 'findings' is standard for a full set of results in a report.

finding.etymology: From Middle English *finden*, Old English *findan*; equivalent to *find* + *-ing*.

senses.definition: The quality of being finical.

core.definition: The quality of being overly fussy, particular or hard to please about small details.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on KAL, the third syllable. The first two syllables are short and quick, and the final -ity is a reduced ih-tee sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It suggests excessive fussiness that can irritate others.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use finicality in everyday speech, where fussiness or pickiness is more natural. It appears mainly in literary criticism or formal writing to describe an author or critic who is too concerned with minor refinements. Using it casually may sound stiff or overly bookish.

distinctions.note: Fussiness is the everyday word for being hard to satisfy. Finicality is more literary and suggests excessive refinement.
Precision is a positive quality of accuracy. Finicality is negative and implies caring too much about trivial details.

examples.professional: Her finicality about formatting slowed the review, but it caught several real errors.
examples.analytical: The essayist's finicality of diction reveals an anxiety about being misunderstood.

nuance.analogy: Finicality is like a jeweler who keeps polishing a stone that already shines, unable to leave it alone.
nuance.etymology: From finical, from fine.
common_mistakes: Confusing finicality with finesse, which means skillful and subtle handling.
Using it for everyday pickiness; fussiness or pickiness is the normal American choice.

senses.definition: The caste of clergy in medieval and early modern society, and in particular in France prior to 1789, as distinct from the nobility and the commoners.
senses.example: In eighteenth-century France, the clergy formed the First Estate, above the nobility and commoners.

core.definition: The clergy as the top class of medieval and early modern French society, before the 1789 Revolution.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on STAYT. The 'ih' in the second word is a reduced, quick vowel, and the t is a clear American t.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a historical term used in academic writing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'first estate' in history classes and academic writing about pre-revolutionary France. In everyday talk you would not hear it, and you would just say 'the clergy' or 'the church.' Pair it with 'second estate' (the nobility) and 'third estate' (commoners) when discussing the French social order.

distinctions.note: 'Clergy' is the general word for church leaders; 'first estate' is the historical legal class in France.
'Aristocracy' means the ruling class by birth; 'first estate' specifically means the clergy.
'Estate' alone can mean property or a large house; 'first estate' means a social class.

examples.everyday: My daughter's history homework is about the first estate, so we've been reading about French clergy together.
examples.professional: In the syllabus, the first estate is covered alongside the nobility and commoners in unit two.
examples.analytical: The privileges of the first estate, including exemption from most direct taxation, became a central grievance before the Revolution of 1789.

nuance.analogy: Like the floors of an old building, each estate was a separate level with its own rights and duties.
nuance.etymology: 'First' from Old English fyrst plus 'estate' from Old French estat, meaning 'condition or status'.
common_mistakes: Using 'estate' to mean property, as in a house or land, when the historical sense is social rank.
Thinking 'first estate' means the most important person, when it refers to a class.

senses.definition: A measure of the amount of information that an observable random variable X carries about an unknown parameter θ of a distribution that models X. Formally, it is the variance of the score, or the expected value of the observed information.

core.definition: A measure of how much information an observable random variable carries about an unknown parameter of its distribution; it equals the variance of the score.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on FISH in Fisher, and on MAY in information, with the other syllables light. The t in information is pronounced as 'sh', so the ending sounds like 'shun'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a precise technical term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this term in statistics, machine learning and econometrics, especially in discussions of estimation and efficiency. It is named after the statistician Ronald A. Fisher and is rarely used in ordinary conversation. In textbooks you will often see expected and observed versions of it.

distinctions.note: Shannon information measures uncertainty or surprise in a random variable; Fisher information measures how sharply data can pin down an unknown parameter.
Expected Fisher information is the average over possible data; observed Fisher information uses the data actually collected.

examples.everyday: My friend in graduate school keeps talking about Fisher information, and I can only follow that it's about how precise a measurement can be.
examples.professional: Our estimator's variance is close to the inverse of the Fisher information, so it is nearly efficient for this model.
examples.analytical: The Cramér-Rao bound states that the variance of any unbiased estimator of θ is at least the reciprocal of the Fisher information.

nuance.analogy: Like the sharpness of a camera lens: the more sharply the data focus on a parameter, the more information the image carries.
nuance.etymology: Named after the statistician Ronald A. Fisher, who introduced the concept in the early 1920s.
common_mistakes: Saying 'a Fisher information' as if it were countable; it is an uncountable noun
Stressing the wrong syllable, as in fi-SHER, when the name is FISH-er

fisher-information.etymology: Named after the statistician Ronald Fisher.

senses.definition: An act of throwing, often violently.
senses.example: With one fling of his arm, the fisherman sent the net spinning across the water.

senses.definition: An act of moving the limbs or body with violent movements, especially in a dance.
senses.example: the fling of a horse

senses.definition: An act or period of unrestrained indulgence, enthusiasm, or both.
senses.example: After exams, the students enjoyed one wild fling before settling into summer jobs.

senses.definition: A short romantic, oftentimes sexual, relationship.
senses.example: a summer fling

senses.definition: An attempt, a try.
senses.example: give it a fling

senses.definition: A lively Scottish country dance.
senses.example: the Highland fling

senses.definition: A party, especially a dance party.
senses.example: a spring fling

senses.definition: To throw with violence or quick movement; to hurl.
senses.example: The coach flung his clipboard onto the bench in frustration after the bad call.

senses.definition: To move (oneself) abruptly or violently; to rush or dash.
senses.example: When the bell rang, the children flung themselves out the door and across the playground.

senses.definition: To utter abusive language; to sneer.
senses.example: The scold began to flout and fling.

core.definition: To throw something forcefully or carelessly, or to move your body suddenly and energetically.

pronunciation.tip: It has one stressed syllable and a short i. Keep the ng as one nasal sound, and do not add a g sound at the end.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to mildly negative, depending on context. A fling as a noun can also mean a brief romance or a wild period.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use fling for throwing things hard, like a ball or a bag, and for a short romantic relationship or a wild period of fun. A fling with someone usually means a casual or brief affair. People often say have a fling or take a fling when talking about a short romance.

distinctions.note: Throw is the general word, while fling suggests more force, carelessness, or abandon.
Toss is lighter and gentler, often for casual passing, while fling implies forceful or wild motion.

examples.everyday: Our dog loves it when I fling the tennis ball across the park.
examples.professional: Please do not fling the draft back at me without comments, because we need a clear review.
examples.analytical: The novel flings its characters into moral chaos, testing how far they will bend before they break.

nuance.analogy: To fling is to let go of something as if you have no need to control where it lands.
nuance.etymology: Middle English flingen, probably of Scandinavian origin.
common_mistakes: Using past tense fling for the participle; the past tense is flung.
Confusing fling with fly, which is about movement through the air rather than force.

fling.etymology: From Middle English *fling*, from the verb.

senses.definition: Growing, thriving, prospering.
senses.example: a flourishing economy

senses.definition: An act or instance of thriving or flowering.
senses.example: The flourishing of the spring garden surprised everyone after such a harsh winter.

senses.definition: A bold, sweeping movement.
senses.example: With a flourishing of his cape, the magician bowed to the cheering audience.

senses.definition: A period of greatest influence.
senses.example: The flourishing of the Dutch Golden Age produced painters we still study today.

senses.definition: A boasting or bragging.
senses.example: His constant flourishing about his salary made the whole team tired of listening to him.

senses.definition: The brandishing of a weapon.
senses.example: The knight's flourishing of his sword drew cheers from the crowd in the square.

core.definition: Growing strongly, healthy, and successful; thriving in a good condition.
